introduction-when-things-go-boom.core: In complex systems failure is certain, not possible. What separates good organisations from bad ones isn't avoiding incidents but detecting, responding to, mitigating and learning from them quickly.

first_principles.problem: Teams treat incidents as rare surprises and improvise every time, so outages last longer and repeat.
truths: Complex systems always contain latent failures.
derivation: **Measure** each lifecycle phase (TTD, TTA, TTM, TTR).

analogy.title: A fire department
analogy.story: Fires will happen; what matters is fast alarms, trained crews and investigation afterwards.
analogy.breaks: Unlike fires, software incidents are often invisible until someone looks.

example.title: A bad deploy

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 25 minutes of impact instead of hours.

example.outcome: incidents are handled as a practised process.

check.q: Why treat incidents as a process rather than surprises?
check.a: Failure is inevitable in complex systems, and a practised process minimises impact.

severity-levels-how-bad-is-it.core: Severity levels (SEV1–SEV4) give everyone the same answer to 'how bad is it?', based on customer impact, scope and business risk. They decide who's paged, how fast, and how communication works.

first_principles.problem: One engineer's 'emergency' is another's 'minor glitch', so responses are mismatched: either over-escalated or ignored.
truths: Response cost should scale with impact.
derivation: **SEV1**: major outage or data loss, all hands, exec comms.
**SEV3**: minor or partial impact, business hours.
**Upgrade or downgrade** as you learn more.

analogy.title: Hospital triage colours
analogy.story: Red, orange, yellow and green tell staff instantly who gets treated first and how.
analogy.breaks: Severity reflects impact, not technical difficulty. A hard bug can still be SEV4.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each gets exactly the response it deserves.

check.q: Should severity be based on technical complexity or customer impact?

the-incident-lifecycle-timeline-metrics.core: An incident's timeline breaks into measurable intervals: TTD (start → detected), TTA (detected → acknowledged), TTM (→ mitigated), TTR (→ resolved). Tracking each shows where the response is slow.

first_principles.problem: A single 'MTTR' number hides whether the problem is slow detection, slow paging or slow fixing.
truths: Each phase has different causes of delay.

analogy.title: A relay race's split times
analogy.story: Knowing each runner's leg time shows exactly where the team loses seconds.
analogy.breaks: Averages (MTTx) hide outliers, so look at distributions and individual incidents.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Investment goes where the time is lost.

points: Each phase has its own fix.

check.q: Which metric best reflects customer pain duration?
check.a: Time to mitigate (TTM), when user impact stops.

phase-1-detection-ttd.core: An incident starts when the system breaks, not when someone notices. Detection speed depends on alerting on symptoms (SLO burn, error rates) rather than waiting for customers to complain.

first_principles.problem: A broken deploy at 10:00 is discovered at 11:30 from a customer tweet.
truths: Alerts must be actionable to be trusted.
derivation: Alert on **user-facing symptoms** (errors, latency, SLO burn rate).
Track **who detected it**: monitoring or customers.

analogy.title: A smoke detector vs. a neighbour calling
analogy.story: You want the detector to sound before the neighbour sees flames.
analogy.breaks: Too many alerts cause fatigue and slow detection too, so alert on what matters.

example.title: An SLO burn-rate alert

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Paged within minutes of a bad deploy.

code.text:
- alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetBurn
  expr: (sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m]))) > 14.4 * 0.001
  for: 2m
  labels: { severity: page }

example.outcome: incidents are found by systems, not customers.

check.q: Why alert on symptoms rather than causes?
check.a: Symptoms reflect actual user impact and catch failures whose causes you didn't anticipate.

phase-2-response-acknowledge-tta.core: Alerts route through PagerDuty or Opsgenie to the on-call engineer, who acknowledges, assesses severity and declares an incident. Schedules, escalation policies and clear expectations keep TTA short.

first_principles.problem: An alert pages someone asleep with no backup, and nobody responds for 30 minutes.
derivation: Define **on-call schedules** with primary and secondary.

analogy.title: A relay of emergency contacts
analogy.story: If the first contact doesn't answer, the call automatically goes to the next.
analogy.breaks: Acknowledging silences the page but doesn't mean progress, so start working immediately.

check.a: It automatically pages the next responder if the current one doesn't acknowledge within a set time.

phase-3-mitigation-ttm-stopping-the-pain.core: First stop the customer impact (roll back, fail over, toggle a flag, scale up, shed load), even before you understand the root cause. Diagnosis comes after the bleeding stops.

first_principles.problem: Engineers spend an hour debugging the root cause while customers keep failing.
truths: Many mitigations don't require understanding the cause.
Recent changes are the most likely culprits.
derivation: Ask **'what changed?'** and roll it back.

analogy.title: First aid before surgery
analogy.story: Stop the bleeding with a tourniquet first; the surgeon investigates afterwards.
analogy.breaks: Some mitigations (failovers) carry their own risk, so practise them.

example.title: Mitigating a memory leak
flow: Debug leak on a staging copy

check.q: Why mitigate before finding the root cause?
check.a: Customer impact continues during diagnosis, and many mitigations (rollback, flags) work without knowing the cause.

phase-4-resolution-ttr-the-permanent-fix.core: After mitigation, resolve: find the underlying causes calmly, implement and verify a permanent fix, remove temporary workarounds, and close the incident, which feeds into the post-incident review.

first_principles.problem: Mitigations like 'rolled back' or 'manually restarted' become permanent, and the incident recurs.
truths: Mitigation isn't the same as a fix.

analogy.title: Fixing the pipe after mopping up the flood
analogy.story: Mopping (mitigation) stops the damage; replacing the pipe (resolution) stops it happening again.
analogy.breaks: Some 'resolutions' need long projects, so track them as action items.

check.q: What's the difference between TTM and TTR?
check.a: TTM is when customer impact stops; TTR is when the underlying issue is permanently fixed.
